title: A Cavendish banana has three sets of chromosomes, so it almost never makes a seed
body: In October 2026 Yelloway, a venture of Chiquita and the breeders KeyGene, announced a fertile Cavendish breeding line; on 22 October the Guardian asked if it could help save the banana ([the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/22/have-scientists-finally-found-a-way-to-save-the-banana-from-disaster)). The Cavendish has three sets of its 11 kinds of chromosome, 33 in all; a wild banana has two ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_acuminata)). Making sex cells halves the chromosomes: pairs split evenly, but a trio sends two copies one way and one the other, so in a simple model only about 1 sex cell in 1,024 is balanced. So it makes almost no seeds, and its fruit grows without pollination. Farmers plant offshoots instead, so every Cavendish is a near-identical clone, open to the same diseases, like TR4, a strain of the Panama disease fungus that felled the Gros Michel banana from the 1950s. Yelloway says its line keeps 100% Cavendish genes and has been crossed with resistant bananas ([FreshPlaza](https://www.freshplaza.com/asia/article/9882446/fertile-cavendish-banana-line-developed-for-disease-resistant-breeding/)); how is not yet published.

slides.prompt: Cavendish bananas have no working seeds. So where does each new Cavendish plant come from?
slides.answer: An offshoot of an older plant
slides.detail: Each new plant sprouts from the base of another, so every Cavendish is a near-identical clone, open to the same diseases.

slides.alt: Animation in a night-green plantation: a slice with no seeds beside a wild one full of them. Clone plants sprout from offshoots and brown together as a fungus spreads. Coloured chromosomes split: pairs evenly, trios two and one; a grid of 1,024 squares has one green. Hand crosses give a seed or two.

slides.prompt: Make sex cells with 2 or 3 chromosome sets. With a Cavendish’s 3 sets of 11 kinds, how many come out balanced?
slides.takeaway: About 1 in 1,024: all 11 trios must split the same way. With pairs every sex cell is balanced, so wild bananas are full of seeds.

left.label: Wild banana
left.text: 2 sets of 11 chromosomes, 22 in all. Pairs split evenly, so its sex cells work, and its fruit is full of hard seeds.

right.label: Cavendish
right.text: 3 sets, 33 in all. Trios can’t split evenly, so its sex cells nearly always come out unbalanced: almost no seeds.

slides.question: Why do a Cavendish banana’s sex cells almost never work?
options: Its chromosome trios can’t split evenly
slides.explanation: Each of its 11 chromosome trios splits two and one, so a sex cell is balanced only if all 11 go the same way: about 1 in 1,024 in a simple model.
